overview.summary: Whether encryption no provider can break is an intolerable investigative gap or the security property everyone depends on.
overview.scope_covered: Access to end-to-end encrypted messages and devices: exceptional-access mandates, on-device scanning, targeted hacking, metadata, and the security costs of each.
overview.scope_excluded: Bulk untargeted surveillance, moderation of lawful speech, cryptographic export controls, data localization, and the quantum threat to today’s ciphers.
overview.why_now: EU negotiators from the Parliament, Council and Commission have settled most of the child sexual abuse regulation, but remain split on whether platform detection stays voluntary or becomes mandatory. Both sides have already agreed any mandate would stop short of end-to-end encrypted services, which leaves open how far detection can reach once encryption is carved out.

stats.label: Drop in child-abuse-material reports to the US clearinghouse · NCMEC, 2023 to 2024
stats.note: Reports fell from 36.2 million in 2023 to 20.5 million in 2024 as Meta encrypted Messenger; NCMEC also names reporting changes elsewhere — counted as incidents, the drop is about 19 percent.
stats.detail: The pattern was not limited to Facebook: Instagram’s reports also fell sharply, from 11.4 million to 3.3 million, while WhatsApp, already end-to-end encrypted throughout both years, held roughly steady at 1.4 to 1.9 million. Electronic service providers accounted for 35.9 million of the 36.2 million reports in 2023 and 20.3 million of the 20.5 million in 2024; the remainder came from the public. In 2025 the aggregate recovered to 21.3 million, of which 21.1 million came from providers, with Facebook’s own reports falling again to 4.9 million while Instagram rose to 3.7 million and WhatsApp to 2.4 million. Alongside Meta’s bundling, NCMEC names several other contributing factors for 2024: platforms including Google, X, Discord, Microsoft and Synchronoss filed 20 percent fewer reports than in 2023, Meta and Google stopped forwarding images that violated their terms of service but did not meet the legal definition of child pornography, and further implementation of end-to-end encryption. NCMEC also cautions that providers face no legal requirement to search for this content proactively, and that no standard governs what a single report must contain, so both the volume and the content of reports vary greatly. Child-safety advocates read the 2024 fall as detection capacity lost to encryption; digital-rights advocates read report volume as a poor proxy for how much abuse content, or how many prosecutable cases, went undetected either way.
stats.source_label: NCMEC, CyberTipline data and reports by electronic service provider, 2023 to 2025

stats.label: Practical attacks on AES-256, as of 2026 · the cipher behind secure messaging
stats.note: No known practical attack can read data properly encrypted with AES-256, the cipher underlying most end-to-end encrypted messaging and device storage.
stats.detail: AES-256 has a keyspace of 2^256 possible keys. The best published shortcuts are biclique attacks, introduced in 2011 and refined since, with the strongest published result still requiring about 2^254.3 operations, only a few times faster than trying every key and nowhere near fast enough to matter, so brute force remains computationally infeasible with any foreseeable hardware. This is why the access debate centers on how a lawful path in is built, whether by backdoor, on-device scanning, or hacking, rather than on whether the underlying cipher itself can be broken.
stats.source_label: Bogdanov, Khovratovich & Rechberger, “Biclique Cryptanalysis of the Full AES” (2011); standard: NIST FIPS 197

stats.label: Countries where Apple pulled full iCloud encryption · UK order, 2025
stats.note: In February 2025 the UK secretly ordered Apple to open encrypted iCloud backups worldwide; Apple pulled the feature for new UK users instead, and appealed.
stats.detail: The notice, issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, sought access to iCloud backups regardless of a user’s nationality or location, not just UK residents’. Public disclosure of the notice’s existence would normally be illegal under the Act; it came to light through press reports on February 7, 2025. Apple disabled the option for new UK users on February 21, 2025, told existing UK users to turn it off, and appealed to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal in March 2025. It is the first publicly confirmed use of this power against a major global encryption feature. In August 2025 the US Director of National Intelligence said the UK had agreed to drop the demand as it applied to Americans’ data. The Home Office then served a fresh notice narrowed to UK users’ data, reported in October 2025, and Apple filed a new challenge against it at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal in August 2026.
stats.source_label: BBC News, “Apple pulls data protection tool after UK government security row” (2025-02-22)

stats.label: Years before the first backdoor mandate collapsed · US Clipper Chip
stats.note: The 1993 Clipper Chip, the first push to mandate a government key in every encryption device, was shown exploitable within two years and was dead by 1996.
stats.detail: Clipper embedded a law-enforcement access key in hardware, escrowed with the government. In 1994, researcher Matt Blaze showed the 16-bit checksum meant to keep that access field trustworthy could be defeated by brute force, letting a device use full encryption while defeating the escrow; a 1995 follow-on showed one device’s access field could be swapped onto another’s traffic. Combined with public backlash and the spread of alternatives like PGP, the chip found essentially no buyers outside the Department of Justice and was abandoned by 1996. It remains the standard historical reference point on both sides of the exceptional-access debate.
stats.source_label: Blaze, “Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard,” ACM CCS 1994

stats.label: Cost to break into one locked iPhone without Apple’s help · FBI, 2016
stats.note: Apple refused a court order to unlock the San Bernardino shooter’s iPhone, so the FBI paid an outside firm to break in: more than $1.3 million, by then director James Comey’s account.
stats.detail: The case followed the December 2015 attack; a magistrate ordered Apple to build bypass software in February 2016, which Apple publicly refused. The government dropped its case in March 2016 after a third party demonstrated an unlocking method. Comey publicly suggested the tool cost more than $1.3 million; the actual figure has never been disclosed, and in 2017 a federal court held that both the vendor’s identity and the amount paid were exempt from FOIA.

stats.label: Years the EU has debated mandatory scanning of encrypted chats · Chat Control proposal
stats.note: The EU has argued since 2022 over whether platforms must scan messages for child abuse material. The Council’s November 2025 position dropped encrypted services from any mandate; by mid-2026 there was still no final text.
stats.detail: The Commission’s original 2022 draft covered end-to-end encrypted services. Opposition built over several years: Denmark dropped mandatory detection obligations from its Council presidency draft in October 2025, and the Council adopted a position in November 2025 excluding end-to-end encrypted communications from mandatory detection technologies, keeping only a voluntary basis. Trilogue negotiations between Parliament, Council, and Commission began in December 2025 and continued into mid-2026, with detection measures still the main point of disagreement.

stats.label: People with end-to-end encrypted messaging by default · WhatsApp and Signal
stats.note: WhatsApp reported 3 billion monthly users in May 2025, all end-to-end encrypted by default; Signal adds roughly 70 million more.
stats.detail: Signal’s user base grew from roughly 20 million monthly users at the end of 2020 to over 40 million by January 2022 and about 70 million by January 2025, with more than 220 million cumulative downloads. This is the population any exceptional-access, scanning, or hacking regime would have to be designed around.
stats.source_label: Wikipedia, WhatsApp (May 2025 MAU); Signal usage figures

stats.label: Years the EU’s mandatory metadata retention law survived · Data Retention Directive
stats.note: The EU’s 2006 mandate that telecoms and internet providers retain everyone’s call, email, and location metadata for up to two years was struck down in 2014.
stats.detail: The European Court of Justice invalidated the directive on April 8, 2014. It was never replaced at EU level, and national retention laws have been challenged before the court repeatedly since. The ruling stands as a limit on how far governments can lean on bulk metadata as a substitute for content access. The US has no comparable nationwide ISP retention law, though NSA bulk metadata programs have operated under separate legal authorities, and countries such as Australia (from 2015, at an estimated AU$189 to 319 million in upfront capital costs, of which the government met AU$131 million) and Russia have kept mandatory retention laws of their own.
stats.source_label: Court of Justice of the European Union, judgment in Digital Rights Ireland, Joined Cases C-293/12 and C-594/12

stats.label: Government spending on spyware in one country · Mexico and NSO Group’s Pegasus, to 2023
stats.note: As of 2023, Mexico’s government had spent more than $60 million on NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, one measure of what targeted device hacking costs at the high end.
stats.detail: Pegasus is a zero-click tool that can read messages, track location, and activate a device’s microphone and camera once installed, without the target clicking anything. Other reported government deals include a $30 million down payment from Estonia (2018); Citizen Lab detected infections across at least 45 countries between 2016 and 2018. Skeptics of hacking as a substitute for mandated access read this cost profile as evidence it can only ever reach a small number of high-value targets; the investigators who back the approach read operations like EncroChat as evidence it scales.

stats.label: Renewed federal contract for phone-unlocking forensic tools · Cellebrite, DHS, 2025
stats.note: Homeland Security renewed an $11 million Cellebrite phone-forensics contract in September 2025, continuing years of federal spending on unlocking seized phones.
stats.detail: Cellebrite’s forensic tools have also been bought by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in contracts as large as $30 to 35 million (2019), and by UK government agencies for a combined $370,000 in 2024. In 2021, security researcher Moxie Marlinspike published vulnerabilities in Cellebrite’s own software, including components years out of date, after which Cellebrite narrowed its support for extracting data from current iPhones. The company’s trajectory illustrates both the recurring cost of targeted-hacking tools as an alternative to a mandated backdoor and the limits on how reliably such tools keep pace with newer device encryption.

questions.text: Can lawful access to encrypted content be engineered without creating a vulnerability that others can find and exploit?
questions.why: Both sides accept that an access mechanism must not become a general vulnerability; they split on whether decades of failed designs prove that is impossible or only that it is unsolved.
questions.detail:
Every exceptional-access proposal studied since the 1990s Clipper Chip has introduced a new server, key-escrow system, or duplicate key that becomes the highest-value target on the network; break that one point and every conversation it protects is exposed at once. Landmark technical assessments, from the original crypto wars through the 2015 “Keys Under Doormats” report, concluded that no design has separated “accessible to a court order” from “accessible to anyone who compromises that mechanism,” an objection this camp holds no published proposal has since answered.

Proponents note that plenty of security-critical systems already carry a trusted, audited exception without collapsing, code-signing keys, certificate authorities, cloud providers that can produce unencrypted backups, and argue the real obstacle is political will and engineering investment, not a proof of impossibility. “No solution yet found” is not the same claim as “no solution possible,” they argue, and companies already hold and can be compelled to produce plaintext in many contexts today without a resulting wave of unrelated breaches.

questions.text: How much serious crime actually goes unsolved because of encryption, rather than being solved by other investigative means?
questions.why: Both camps cite the same “going dark” claim from very different baselines, and no agency publishes an audited count of cases lost to encryption rather than solved another way.
questions.detail:
Investigators and prosecutors describe a rising share of cases, from child exploitation rings to terrorism plots, where a seized phone or app is technically inaccessible even with a valid warrant, and argue that publicized cases are the visible tip of a much larger unmeasured problem, since failures to access evidence are rarely logged as a discrete category and often never surface publicly at all.

Skeptics of the “going dark” narrative point to the huge growth in other data streams, carrier records, location history, cloud backups, connected devices, informants, that increasingly fill the gap, and note that some past law-enforcement claims about specific unsolvable-case counts have later been corrected or retracted. Because no public agency publishes a rigorous, audited tally of cases lost specifically to encryption versus cases solved by other means, both camps are extrapolating from selective examples rather than a shared count.

questions.text: Does an individual’s claim to communication no one can read outweigh a society’s claim to execute a lawful warrant?
questions.why: This is the philosophical fork underneath every technical argument: whether a warrant, properly obtained, is owed access as a matter of principle, or whether some communications are legitimately beyond any warrant’s reach.
questions.detail:
For this camp, a warrant has always authorized a search, not guaranteed a result. Locks that cannot be picked, conversations that leave no record, rooms with no listening device, have existed throughout history without being treated as a defect in the rule of law; encryption is simply the modern version of a private conversation that leaves nothing behind for the state to search.

For the opposing camp, a valid warrant is a democratic society’s answer to exactly this tension: a court has already weighed the individual’s privacy against the public interest and ruled that access is justified in this instance, so a technology that can defeat that court order unconditionally substitutes the manufacturer’s judgment for the judiciary’s.

questions.text: Would an access mechanism built by one democracy stay confined to it, or hand authoritarian states a precedent they will demand in turn?
questions.why: The debate turns on whether a mechanism can be legally and technically restricted to democracies with due process, or whether any working exceptional-access system becomes a template every government will point to.
questions.detail:
Mandaters argue this treats every democracy as hostage to the worst government in the world, and that companies already differentiate compliance by jurisdiction, data localization, content takedowns, region-specific privacy defaults, without those systems collapsing into a single global lowest common denominator. A carefully scoped mechanism, they argue, can be paired with legal and technical safeguards that keep it answerable only to the courts that authorized it.

Advocates point to a repeated pattern: laws and technical standards built for one country’s courts have quickly been cited by other governments demanding the same capability for their own purposes, and because the underlying code and hardware are usually global, the same phone, the same app, the same chipset, a company that builds an access mechanism for one legal system has little technical ground left to refuse it to another, however different that government’s due process protections.

questions.text: Can on-device scanning be held to one category of illegal content, or does building the capability make scope expansion inevitable?
questions.why: The dispute is whether a scanning system built to match one narrow, universally condemned category of content can be kept there, or whether the infrastructure itself invites new categories once it exists.
questions.detail:
Proponents argue scope is a policy and legal choice, not a technical inevitability: narrow, independently audited matching against a court-supervised hash list, rather than open-ended content classification, can be constrained the same way other narrowly defined surveillance powers are constrained, by statute, oversight, and transparency reporting, with the technology itself agnostic to whatever list it is pointed at.

Critics point to a consistent trajectory in comparable systems: content-scanning and filtering infrastructure built for one purpose, copyright, terrorism content, national censorship, has repeatedly been expanded to new categories once regulators or courts direct it, because the hard technical and organizational work, the hash lists, the review pipeline, the on-device hooks, already exists and just needs a new target plugged in. A major platform’s proposal to scan for known abuse material was shelved after researchers showed how the same architecture could be repurposed for other content by policy change alone.

questions.text: Is targeted device hacking a real substitute for mandated access at the volume of ordinary criminal casework, or only for high-value targets?
questions.why: The question is one of scale: whether the exploits, expertise and time that targeted hacking requires can ever be routine tools for ordinary casework, or whether they only work for the handful of cases that justify the cost.
questions.detail:
Proponents counter that this is the point, not a flaw: a warrant-authorized, targeted intrusion into one suspect’s device leaves everyone else’s security untouched, unlike a mandated backdoor that weakens every user’s security regardless of suspicion. They argue specialized units, shared exploit infrastructure and growing commercial tooling are already lowering the cost and expanding how far down the caseload targeted hacking can reach.

Skeptics of hacking as a substitute argue that it depends on unpatched vulnerabilities that are expensive to find or buy, that degrade the moment they are used and detected, and that require specialized skills most police departments do not have in-house. On this account it is used sparingly, reserved for terrorism, organized crime or the highest-priority cases where the cost is justified, while the overwhelming volume of routine cases, local burglaries, ordinary drug cases, domestic violence, never reach that threshold.

questions.text: Who should carry the residual risk: the people whose data an access mechanism would expose, or the victims of crimes that go unsolved without one?
questions.why: Once the technical and legal arguments are exhausted, the remaining question is a values choice about who should absorb the harm the debate cannot fully resolve either way.
questions.detail:
The Exceptional Access Mandater and Client-Side Scanning camps argue that the current default already asks victims and their families to bear the entire cost of an unsolved case, an outcome that is concentrated, severe and often irreversible, while the risk to general users from a well-designed access mechanism is diffuse, probabilistic and mitigated by oversight. A society that can act to prevent concrete, ongoing harm but chooses not to, they argue, is also making a values choice, not a neutral one.

The Digital Rights Defender and Metadata Sufficiency camps argue that weakening encryption spreads a risk, that a mechanism might be misused or breached, across every user of a system, including the most vulnerable ones, journalists, abuse survivors, dissidents, while the benefit accrues only in the cases where lawful access would actually have mattered. Spreading harm broadly and thinly to avoid a smaller number of concentrated, unsolved cases, in this view, is not a defensible trade.

positions.name: No-Backdoor Cryptographer
positions.steelman: Math grants no exceptions for good guys: build the door, someone else finds the key.
positions.description: Security is not a dial that can be turned down for law enforcement and stay put for everyone else. Every exceptional-access design studied so far has needed key escrow, weaker forward secrecy, or new code paths: more attack surface, not less. Salt Typhoon showed the failure mode is real, reaching the very lawful-intercept systems built to serve court-authorized wiretaps.
positions.detail:
The canonical text is Keys Under Doormats (Abelson, Anderson, Bellovin, Benaloh, Blaze, Diffie, Gilmore, Green, Landau, Neumann, Rivest, Schiller, Schneier, Specter and Weitzner; Journal of Cybersecurity, 2015), a direct rebuttal to the FBI’s renewed “going dark” push under Director James Comey. It updated the field’s founding argument from the 1990s Clipper Chip fight: that any mandated exceptional-access mechanism forces a system away from modern security practice, in particular forward secrecy, and replaces it with centralized key material that becomes the single highest-value target on the network. The paper does not claim access is impossible to build; it documents that no proposal has answered how it would be built without those costs, across a decade of governments asking.

That prediction has since been borne out operationally rather than theoretically. Salt Typhoon, the Chinese state-linked intrusion disclosed in 2024, sat inside AT&T, Verizon and other US carriers for what officials assessed was one to two years before discovery, reaching the lawful-intercept systems installed decades earlier specifically to give law enforcement access, and giving foreign intelligence a live feed of the exact metadata and, in some cases, content those backdoors existed to collect for police. This camp reads Australia’s Assistance and Access Act 2018 as the clearest legislative case study of the same dynamic, arguing that a compelled technical-assistance notice cannot be scoped to a single target without touching the software update or authentication mechanism every other user of that product relies on.

The camp’s internal debate is less about whether backdoors are safe, where no significant faction inside it argues otherwise, than about which fallback investigative methods to endorse in their place: cryptographers like Susan Landau argue for redirecting law enforcement toward metadata analysis and traditional forensics, while others emphasize targeted device exploitation under warrant as the technically sound substitute. Signal’s Meredith Whittaker and the Electronic Frontier Foundation carry the argument into present-day legislative fights: Signal said publicly in 2023 that it would leave the UK market rather than comply with the Online Safety Bill’s scanning powers, and the EFF has called the US EARN IT Act a direct threat to constitutional protections for free speech and expression. Each such bill is treated by this camp as Clipper Chip and Keys Under Doormats revisited under a new name.
positions.proponents: Bruce Schneier, Matthew Green, Susan Landau, Whitfield Diffie, Ross Anderson, Matt Blaze, Meredith Whittaker (Signal), Electronic Frontier Foundation
positions.representative_note: Peer-reviewed paper by 15 leading cryptographers and security researchers, Journal of Cybersecurity, the field’s standing rebuttal to every renewed exceptional-access proposal since.

positions.name: Exceptional Access Mandater
positions.steelman: A lawful warrant should open the door, not stop at a vendor’s design choice.
positions.description: Democratic societies work because no space is beyond a lawful warrant: not a house, not a bank vault, not a phone. Encryption built so that not even the provider can comply turns judicial power into a dead letter, and the people who pay are victims. Warranted access is something engineering teams should solve for, like reliability or battery life, not market against.
positions.detail:
The lineage runs from the 1990s Clipper Chip fight through the 2016 San Bernardino case, where a court order compelling Apple to write unlock software was dropped only because the FBI found another way in, not because the demand was wrong. The camp’s most developed technical answer is GCHQ’s 2018 “ghost protocol,” proposed by Ian Levy and Crispin Robinson, which would add a silent, warrant-authorized participant to an existing encrypted conversation rather than hand over master keys, arguing that the “nobody but the parties can read this” promise already has an exception, the provider who can push a compromised app update, that a lawful process could simply formalize. Australia’s 2018 Assistance and Access Act and the UK’s Investigatory Powers Act, with its judicial “double lock” on warrants, are held up as working proof that a statutory access regime can operate without the sky falling.

The camp splits on mechanism: some back a legislative mandate with fixed technical requirements, like the US Lawful Access to Encrypted Data Act, while others prefer case-by-case compelled assistance litigated fresh each time, the Apple precedent, wary that a standing mandate is itself the vulnerability. What unites them is a rejection of the cryptographers’ “any backdoor is everyone’s backdoor” framing as a design failure to be solved rather than a law of physics: warrant-gated access is achievable, they argue, if a vendor is required to engineer for it from the start instead of retrofitting it under subpoena. In October 2020 the governments of the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India and Japan endorsed exactly that framing in a joint statement calling on industry to embed public-safety capability into system design.

The camp now argues from a record rather than a forecast. Facebook’s own reports to NCMEC’s CyberTipline fell from 17.8 million in 2023 to 8.6 million in 2024 and 4.9 million in 2025, across the period Meta made end-to-end encryption the default on Messenger, and mandaters read that as the measured cost of a rollout they warned about in advance. They read the UK’s February 2025 technical capability notice the same way: a democracy’s lawful order working as designed, statutory, judicially supervised and served on one company, met by a vendor that chose to pull a product feature from that market rather than comply. That, mandaters argue, is exactly the vendor design choice their case is about, since the access was refused by a business decision and not by mathematics.
positions.proponents: Christopher Wray, William Barr, James Comey, Priti Patel, Ian Levy, Crispin Robinson (GCHQ), U.S. Lawful Access to Encrypted Data Act (Sens. Graham, Cotton, Blackburn)
positions.representative_name: GCHQ’s Ian Levy and Crispin Robinson
positions.representative_note: Authors of the 2018 paper proposing a warrant-gated “ghost” participant silently added to an encrypted call or chat, arguing exceptional access is an engineering problem to be solved, not a cryptographic impossibility.

positions.name: Digital Rights Defender
positions.steelman: Secret demands in one democracy become every government’s precedent.
positions.description: Start with who depends on unbreakable encryption: journalists protecting sources, dissidents, LGBTQ+ people where their identity is still a crime, abuse survivors hiding from a partner who knows their passwords. No access mechanism stays one democracy’s secret. The UK’s secret 2025 order to Apple was contestable only because it leaked, and the power behind it is unchanged.
positions.detail:
The modern version of this argument dates to the May 2015 report to the UN Human Rights Council by David Kaye, then Special Rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, which concluded that encryption and anonymity enable people to exercise the rights to freedom of opinion and expression and so deserve strong protection, and that states should avoid all measures that weaken the security individuals enjoy online, naming backdoors, weak encryption standards and key escrows, with journalists, human rights defenders and dissidents having the most to lose. Three years later, Australia’s Assistance and Access Act 2018 became the case study rights groups still cite: a liberal democracy legislating exceptional access, they warned, would hand illiberal governments a template to point to. That warning aged into fact when India wrote a traceability mandate for WhatsApp into its 2021 IT Rules, and again in February 2025 when the UK used its Investigatory Powers Act to serve Apple a secret order demanding a backdoor into encrypted iCloud backups worldwide. Apple’s answer was to withdraw the feature for UK users rather than build the door, then appeal the order to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal. In August 2025 the US Director of National Intelligence said the UK was dropping the demand, without any public account of what remains of the notice, before a narrowed order on UK users’ data revived the fight that October and drew a fresh Apple challenge in August 2026.

The camp is not united on tactics. Some organizations, including the Global Encryption Coalition’s more than 350 members, steered by the Center for Democracy & Technology, Global Partners Digital, Mozilla, the Internet Freedom Foundation and the Internet Society, work the legislative and multilateral track: filing UN submissions, lobbying against bills like the UK’s Online Safety Act and the EU’s proposed chat control regulation. Others favor exit over negotiation. Signal’s leadership has said publicly the organization would rather leave a market than weaken its encryption, a stance some allies worry cedes the field to less principled competitors when the government asking is a G7 democracy rather than an obvious autocracy. A second fault line runs through client-side scanning proposals pitched as a compromise: most of this camp treats scanning content on the device before it is encrypted as the same backdoor under a different name, since it still requires building a surveillance capability a government can later expand.

The strongest evidence is who actually turns up as the casualty once an access capability exists. The Committee to Protect Journalists has documented reporters jailed or exposed after states obtained their communications, and the 2021 Pegasus Project, coordinated by Forbidden Stories with forensic analysis by Amnesty International’s Security Lab, whose methodology Citizen Lab independently peer-reviewed, found spyware infections on the phones of journalists and human rights defenders across multiple countries once a targeted-access tool existed to be aimed at them. Advocacy groups working with domestic violence survivors have separately made the case that strong encryption is what keeps a coercive partner from reading a survivor’s messages once that partner has physical access to a shared device: weakening it for law enforcement does not distinguish between a warrant and a stalker holding someone’s phone.
positions.proponents: Electronic Frontier Foundation, Access Now, Privacy International, Global Encryption Coalition, Human Rights Watch, Committee to Protect Journalists, Meredith Whittaker (Signal Foundation), David Kaye (former UN Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression)
positions.representative_note: Runs a 24/7 Digital Security Helpline for journalists, activists and human rights defenders facing state surveillance and hacking, and coordinates global encryption advocacy across the #KeepItOn coalition.

positions.name: Client-Side Scanning Proponent
positions.steelman: Scan on the device, before it’s sealed: the encryption in transit stays intact.
positions.description: Encryption protects a message in transit and storage; it was never a promise that the device writing it is unaccountable. Client-side scanning checks an image against a list of known abuse material before the message is sealed, leaving transport and storage exactly as opaque as before. It is the detection layer already running today, and declining to deploy it has its own victims.
positions.detail:
Perceptual hashing became the workhorse of this position in 2009, when Microsoft and computer scientist Hany Farid built PhotoDNA: a fingerprinting method that flags known illegal images without any human viewing them first. Apple’s 2021 CSAM Detection proposal was this camp’s most concrete design for the encrypted era, matching that same style of hash against NCMEC’s list entirely on-device, before an image ever left for iCloud, with no content decrypted or reviewed unless a match threshold was crossed. To proponents, that architecture answered the core objection before it was raised: nothing about the transport or storage encryption changed, and no new content was exposed to the provider.

The camp did not emerge from that unscathed. Apple paused the rollout in September 2021 and formally cancelled the iCloud matching component in December 2022 after sustained privacy backlash, the central objection being that the hash list and matching infrastructure were themselves a standing capability a government could redirect; proponents largely read that as a communications failure and a coalition loss, not a technical refutation, and the same design has resurfaced in the EU’s CSAM Regulation debate, pushed by child-protection groups including Thorn, ECPAT and WeProtect Global Alliance as a legal mandate rather than a voluntary feature. Inside the camp, the live argument is narrower than critics assume: not whether to scan, but who curates the hash list, whether it should ever extend past graphic CSAM to other illegal categories, and whether independent audit of the list can be built without recreating the opacity the design is meant to avoid.

The strongest evidence this camp points to is operational, not theoretical: hash-matching systems already run across the major platforms and generate the tips that let NCMEC and law enforcement identify victims, and this camp reads the fall in reporting from Meta’s platforms after its December 2023 rollout, Facebook from 17.8 million reports to 8.6 million and again to 4.9 million in 2025, as exactly that channel closing. That, to this camp, is the actual trade being debated: a working, narrowly targeted detection mechanism against a channel going permanently dark to it.
positions.proponents: Hany Farid, Thorn, NCMEC, WeProtect Global Alliance, Apple (2021 CSAM Detection proposal), ECPAT
positions.representative_note: Child-safety technology nonprofit, co-founded by Ashton Kutcher and Demi Moore, that builds Safer, a perceptual-hash and classifier CSAM detection product licensed to platforms, and lobbies for detection mandates in the EU’s CSAM Regulation.

positions.name: Targeted Hacking Investigator
positions.steelman: One warrant, one endpoint, zero backdoors in everyone else’s encryption.
positions.description: The state does not have to weaken the mathematics everyone relies on to catch the person using it. A warrant to enter one suspect’s phone leaves the cryptography protecting billions of other devices untouched. French investigators implanted malware on EncroChat’s infrastructure in 2020; the UK arm alone produced more than 3,100 arrests by October 2023, with no change to consumer encryption.
positions.detail:
The position takes its name from a 2014 Northwestern Journal of Technology and Intellectual Property paper, “Lawful Hacking: Using Existing Vulnerabilities for Wiretapping on the Internet,” in which Bellovin, Blaze, Clark and Landau argued the FBI’s “going dark” problem could be solved with tools investigators already had, not a legislated backdoor. The argument got an unplanned real-world test two years later: when the FBI sought a court order forcing Apple to help unlock the San Bernardino shooter’s iPhone, the bureau withdrew its case in March 2016 after a third party supplied a working exploit instead, at a cost then-director James Comey put at more than $1.3 million, with later reporting identifying the Australian security firm Azimuth Security as the source of the tool. Even Michael Hayden, former director of both the NSA and the CIA, sided with the hackers over the bureau’s own lawyers, arguing law enforcement should give up some ground on access to preserve cybersecurity broadly.

The camp is not united on how the government should get its exploits in the first place. Some proponents want agencies to acquire zero-days and run each one through the Vulnerabilities Equities Process to decide case by case whether to disclose or retain it; others argue that stockpiling is itself the systemic risk the position claims to avoid, pointing to the NSA’s own EternalBlue exploit, which leaked in 2017 and was repurposed within weeks for the WannaCry ransomware outbreak. A parallel fight plays out over how broad a single hacking warrant can be: the FBI’s 2015 Playpen investigation used one Virginia warrant to deploy malware against site visitors worldwide, and became the leading example in the fight over the 2016 amendment to Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 that now lets a single warrant cover hacking targets whose location has been disguised; an appeals court later held that particular warrant invalid, though the evidence was allowed to stand under the good-faith exception.

The strongest answer to the objection that this only works for high-value targets is scale, not exception. The UK’s Investigatory Powers Act 2016 wrote “equipment interference” warrants into ordinary law rather than treating device hacking as a covert carve-out, and Europol’s EncroChat and Sky ECC operations show the technique running as full-scale organized-crime enforcement, not a one-off against a single suspect’s phone. Proponents read that record as proof the trade-off is real and worth making: harder, slower, warrant-bound access to the guilty, instead of a structural weakness sitting in the software of the innocent, waiting for whoever finds it first.
positions.proponents: Susan Landau, Matt Blaze, Steven M. Bellovin, Sandy Clark, Alex Stamos, Orin Kerr, UK Investigatory Powers Act 2016 (equipment interference warrants), Europol EncroChat operation
positions.representative_note: Tufts University cybersecurity and policy scholar; co-author of the 2014 paper “Lawful Hacking” and the book Listening In, the position’s central intellectual case

positions.name: Metadata Sufficiency Analyst
positions.steelman: The gap was never the law: it’s underfunded forensics labs and slow provider cooperation.
positions.description: Solving crimes matters more than protecting any one technique, and investigators already reach a lot: cloud accounts, app metadata, location history, device pairings, networked sensors, much of it retained for billing reasons anyway. Berkman Klein’s 2016 Don’t Panic report found no single choke point closing off investigations. Where cases stall, the fix is funding and process.
positions.detail:
The argument has a specific origin. Peter Swire and Kenesa Ahmad set it out early, cataloging what had changed since the wiretap laws of the analog telephone era were written. Where a 1990s investigator had a phone line and not much else, today’s investigator can draw on cloud storage, app-level logs, location history, social media, and always-on device telemetry: an order-of-magnitude expansion in discoverable data that the FBI’s going dark framing never accounted for.

The 2016 Don’t Panic report from the Berkman Klein Center’s Berklett Cybersecurity Project pushed the case further, projecting that the Internet of Things would add networked microphones, cameras, and location beacons to cars, appliances, and utility meters, each a fresh data source with no relationship to whether a given messaging app is end-to-end encrypted. It also made a simpler point: providers retain unencrypted metadata, who contacted whom, when, from where, for how long, for their own billing and engineering reasons, independent of any privacy decision they make about content. Until Apple made end-to-end encrypted iCloud backup optional in December 2022, the default backup for the world’s most popular smartphone line handed most message content to legal process anyway.

The camp’s real split is over what its own argument licenses. If metadata, cloud records and device telemetry are rich enough to replace content access, they are also rich enough to be intrusive on their own terms, which is why Landau and Julian Sanchez pair the argument with limits on retention and legal process while Swire’s version leans on the sheer growth in discoverable data. The camp is likewise not united on whether going dark is spin throughout or a real but narrower problem for specific case types, such as a locally stored device with no cloud backup.
positions.proponents: Peter Swire, Susan Landau, Berkman Klein Center Berklett Cybersecurity Project, Matthew Olsen, Julian Sanchez (Cato Institute)
positions.representative_note: Georgia Tech scholar and member of the 2013 presidential intelligence review group; his 2011 paper with Kenesa Ahmad recast going dark as a golden age for surveillance.

crux.lead: Nobody here disputes the warrant. What splits the field is where it can be executed.
crux.subtitle: Four camps put it somewhere different: the provider’s protocol, the device before sealing, one suspect’s phone, the records already held. Two say the mechanism is the harm, wherever it sits.
crux.empirical: Then it turns on the record: whether an exceptional-access design can be built that survives adversarial review, whether scanning stays confined to one content category at scale, whether warranted hacking reaches ordinary casework volume rather than priority targets, and how many cases genuinely stall on content alone.
crux.values: Then it turns on who carries risk that cannot be engineered away: the people an access mechanism would expose, among them journalists and abuse survivors, or the victims of crimes left unsolved without one. Beneath that sits a question no dataset answers: whether a capability built under one democracy’s courts stays inside them.

Camp parity is the strongest thing about this draft. All six camps get an in-voice steelman a proponent would put on a banner, a canonical text (Keys Under Doormats; GCHQ's 2018 ghost paper; Kaye's 2015 UN report; PhotoDNA/Apple's 2021 design; the 2014 "Lawful Hacking" paper; Don't Panic), named living proponents, a real internal fault line, and a "strongest evidence" paragraph. Nobody is sourced from their opponents' characterization, and no camp's description contains a rebuttal smuggled in as fact. The Client-Side Scanning card is the usual place these topics strawman, and it does not: Apple's cancellation is faced squarely and read as a coalition loss rather than a technical refutation, which is what the camp actually says.

Shared sections hold. Basics gives both readings where a stat is contested (the NCMEC fall, the Pegasus cost profile) and both-sides-reference-it framing where it is historical (Clipper). The question "why" lines are symmetric, and the paragraph pivots alternate which side speaks first. The lean values worried me at first (four empirical questions all leaning against the access side), but I traced lean_pct_a through topics/models.py and templates/topics/components/_qlean.html: the editorial estimate never renders — percentages and the bar appear only once reader votes cross the threshold — so it cannot read as a house verdict on the page.

CRUX: genuine. "Nobody here disputes the warrant. What splits the field is where it can be executed" names an axis rather than declaring a winner, and it survives the multi-camp test: the subtitle gives four distinct loci (provider protocol / device before sealing / one suspect's phone / records already held) that map cleanly onto Mandater, Client-Side Scanning, Targeted Hacking and Metadata Sufficiency, with the two rejecting camps located separately. That is six camps placed, not a binary. The empirical and values columns each carry both directions with no thumb on the scale. My one reservation is a phrase, not a structure — see note 4.

MISSING CAMP: none blocking. WebSearch was spent session-wide (1500/1500) on my first call, so I ran the prescribed WebFetch fallback across landscape sources. The one position I found that is not represented is the Carnegie Encryption Working Group's 2019 middle (narrow the fight to lawful access to data at rest on seized phones via on-device escrow, 23 members incl. Jim Baker, Chris Inglis, Rivest, Felten, Landau). I could not establish current organized proponency for it, and the live 2025-26 fights I checked (UK technical capability notice, Canada's Bill C-22 Part 2, the EU CSAM trilogue) are mandate-shaped and land inside camps already on the page. A traceability-mandate position (India's IT Rules) similarly folds into the Mandater camp's compelled-assistance wing.

Load-bearing claims I verified rather than assumed, weighted toward the pro-access side since a wrong fact there would tilt the page: the 70%/12 million figure is verbatim in the October 2019 gov.uk letter ("NCMEC estimates that 70% of Facebook's reporting – 12 million reports globally – would be lost"); the 2025 per-ESP counts are exact against NCMEC's own PDF (Facebook 4,907,710, Instagram 3,673,045, WhatsApp 2,355,302, 21.3M total with 21.1M from ESPs); the October 2020 international statement is correctly counted at seven signatories plus four later joiners (Singapore, Georgia, Ecuador, Jordan — 11 total); Salt Typhoon's CALEA compromise and the one-to-two-year dwell assessment check out; Operation Venetic's 3,100 arrests and 1,240 convictions by 9 October 2023 check out; the Global Encryption Coalition's 400+ members across 103 countries and its five-organization steering committee check out; the Hayden quote is as David Cole reported it; the why_now matches the current Chat Control state (both institutions converged on excluding E2EE, detection-order mandate still the live split); the Bill C-22 action link resolves to the April 2026 open letter it describes.

One cross-cutting observation that is outside my dimension and is NOT a blocking finding from me: eight of the ten Basics stats cite Wikipedia as the rendered source. The published corpus does tolerate this (frontier-ai-regulation ships 4 of 10), so it is not without precedent, but it is double the worst published case and the Basics ladder prefers official or peer-reviewed secondary sources. I verified the substance of several of these independently and found them accurate; flagging it for the fact critic and the human rather than blocking on someone else's dimension.
notes: Emphasis asymmetry in the position cards: descriptions run 817 to 1396 characters against the 800-1000 house norm recorded in research/workflows/budgets.py. The two longest are both encryption-protective (Digital Rights Defender 1396, Metadata Sufficiency Analyst 1336) and the shortest is Exceptional Access Mandater (817), the second-largest camp by prevalence. Crux subtitle: "Two say the mechanism is the harm, wherever it sits" lands immediately after four enumerated locations, two of which (one suspect's phone, the records already held) the No-Backdoor camp's own detail endorses as its preferred fallbacks. Question 1's second paragraph is the only camp-facing paragraph in the questions section that argues without a named example — code-signing keys and certificate authorities in the abstract, against a paragraph above it that names Keys Under Doormats. Action affordances: four cards serve encryption-protective camps (EFF, the Global Encryption Coalition letter, the Signal donation, the R Street piece) against two on the access side, and the only donate card is Signal's. STEELMAN REVIEW — "Encryption vs. Lawful Access"

VERDICT ON THE CORE QUESTION: all six camps are genuinely steelmanned. Every steelman line is a banner a real proponent would sign, each description leads with the camp's own strongest framing rather than an opponent's characterization, and each camp is sourced from its own authoritative texts (Keys Under Doormats for the cryptographers; Levy & Robinson's Lawfare piece and the 2019 Zuckerberg letter for the mandaters; Kaye's A/HRC/29/32 and the Pegasus Project for the rights camp; PhotoDNA and Apple's own design for the scanning camp; Bellovin/Blaze/Clark/Landau's "Lawful Hacking" and EncroChat for the hacking camp; Don't Panic and Swire for the metadata camp). Camp coverage is complete: the four camps that locate the warrant somewhere (provider protocol, device pre-seal, one endpoint, records already held) plus the two that say the mechanism is itself the harm, spanning -3 to +3. No missing major constituency, no house verdict, no forced 50/50 — the leans run 78/22 and 80/20 where the field genuinely is lopsided, and they cut in both directions (Q3 and Q7 favor the warrant side; Q1, Q2, Q4, Q5 favor the security side). The crux is the strongest element in the draft: it names the real axis without adjudicating it.

FACT VERIFICATION. WebSearch budget was exhausted for this session at the first call, so I verified everything through WebFetch plus direct primary-document retrieval (curl + pdftotext) rather than search. Every load-bearing claim I checked held, several verbatim:
- NCMEC: pulled NCMEC's own 2023/2024/2025 ESP PDFs and the 2024 and 2025 annual reports. Facebook 17,838,422 → 8,590,357 → 4,907,710; Instagram 11,430,007 → 3,320,008 → 3,673,045; WhatsApp 1,389,618 → 1,851,086 → 2,355,302; ESP totals 35,944,826 / 20,348,306 / 21,181,300; totals 36.2M / 20.5M / 21.3M; the Meta bundling feature, the 29.2M incident figure and "approximately 7 million fewer incidents"; the 20% decline from Google, X, Discord, Microsoft and Synchronoss; Meta and Google dropping ToS-only images; "no legal requirements regarding proactive efforts." All exact. The ranked series (Instagram 71%, Facebook 52%, ESPs 43%) computes correctly.
- The mandaters' headline number is verbatim from the source PDF: "NCMEC estimates that 70% of Facebook's reporting – 12 million reports globally – would be lost" (4 October 2019).
- Salt Typhoon inside CALEA request systems, "one to two years prior to its discovery"; Keys Under Doormats, 15 named authors, Journal of Cybersecurity 2015, forward secrecy and concentrated key material; Levy & Robinson, Lawfare, 29 Nov 2018; Operation Venetic 3,100+ arrests / 1,240 convictions as of 9 Oct 2023 and the Lille authorization; "Lawful Hacking," NJTIP vol. 12 (2014), all four authors; Comey's $1.3M and Azimuth Security; Hayden's "give up some things in law enforcement... to preserve... our cybersecurity"; Playpen, the EDVA warrant, Rule 41, and the Eleventh Circuit holding the warrant invalid with good-faith admission; Kaye A/HRC/29/32 (22 May 2015) including the near-verbatim "avoid all measures that weaken the security... such as backdoors, weak encryption standards and key escrows"; Global Encryption Coalition "over 400 members distributed across 103 countries" and all five steering organizations; Don't Panic (1 Feb 2016, Berklett); AES 2^256 keyspace, 2^254.3, no practical attack; Signal 20M/40M+/70M and 220M downloads; Cellebrite $11M DHS 2025, $30–35M ICE 2019, $370K UK 2024, Marlinspike; Chat Control (11 May 2022 proposal covering E2EE, Denmark 30 Oct 2025, Council 26 Nov 2025, trilogues 9 Dec 2025, detection still the open item in 2026, both institutions agreeing E2EE is excluded) — which also confirms the why_now. All four action URLs I could reach are live and correctly described, including the April 2026 Bill C-22 open letter (47 organizations, 37 individuals).

WHAT BLOCKS. Three defects, none of them a strawman, all mechanical to fix. First, four of the seven questions run their two detail paragraphs in the reverse of their lean labels — Q1–Q3 put label_a's argument first, Q4–Q7 put label_b's first. I checked 13 questions across two published topics and the para-1 = label_a mapping holds without exception. On Q7 the paragraphs name no camp at all ("This camp" / "The opposing camp"), so a reader who has learned the convention from Q3 will read the 70% argument off the 30% chip: prevalence gets attached to the wrong side, which is exactly the mechanism this atlas uses to carry asymmetry honestly. Second, the Metadata Sufficiency Analyst's internal-debate passage undercuts its own camp with a non-sequitur and spends the Hayden quote twice in one section in opposite directions — once in the description as the camp's best supporting concession, once in the detail as evidence its contributors are uneasy, with the tension never stated. It is the only camp whose section argues against itself without answering. Third, seven of the ten Basics stats cite Wikipedia; the facts are right (I confirmed them), but tertiary sourcing is below the section-scoped BASICS ladder and appears in zero of the three published topics I sampled, all of which cite official statistics, peer-reviewed literature or primary legal documents. That is a measurable parity gap with a cheap fix: swap each citation to the primary source Wikipedia itself cites.

I checked 13 questions across two published topics (vaccine-mandates, moral-status-of-animals) and the mapping holds without exception there. The lean chips render directly beneath the detail (templates/topics/components/_question.html includes _qlean.html after .qmore), so the reader maps the first paragraph onto the left chip. Q7 is the damaging case: both paragraphs are unnamed ("This camp" / "The opposing camp"), so the 70 percent argument is read off the 30 percent chip. Q4, Q5 and Q6 name their actors in-prose and so mislead less, but they are the same defect and the inconsistency is what teaches the reader the wrong mapping.

Q6: put "Proponents counter that this is the point, not a flaw..." first (Scales = a). Q7: put "The opposing camp argues that the current default already asks victims..." first (Data holders = a). Susan Landau, a Don’t Panic coauthor, has elsewhere stressed how much investigative and intelligence value metadata alone carries, echoing the line former NSA and CIA director Michael Hayden delivered at a 2014 Johns Hopkins debate: “We kill people based on metadata.”" — the same quote already appears in the same camp's description: "at a 2014 Johns Hopkins debate, former NSA and CIA director Michael Hayden said “We kill people based on metadata,” a stronger claim about its investigative value than most privacy advocates make about its risk."

Basics are the facts every camp accepts, and the section-scoped ladder for them is official statistics and peer-reviewed secondary literature, then reputable journalism; Wikipedia is tertiary and sits below that bar. notes: Metadata Sufficiency Analyst steelman: "The gap was never law — it’s underfunded forensics labs and slow provider cooperation." This is a real camp claim but it is the camp's secondary one. The deep layer should carry what the normal layer cannot; hand the repeated material to one level and free the other for the camp's unused material (the IPT's April 2025 ruling that the case's existence could not be kept secret would be a strong addition).

Digital Rights Defender, in-voice: "the order was contestable only because it leaked." Apple did appeal to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and the draft's own detail says so two paragraphs later. "Publicly contestable" is the accurate word and costs nothing.

notes: SELECTION, non-blocking: "People with end-to-end encrypted messaging by default · WhatsApp and Signal" (3 billion+) sits at T2, below the fold. It is the scale stat the whole debate is designed around — its own detail says so ("the population any exceptional-access, scanning, or hacking regime would have to be designed around"). The T1 six are all strong so this is not a misplacement, but if any swap is made, this is the strongest promotion candidate (the FBI $1.3M unlock cost is partly duplicated by the Targeted Hacking steelman and the Cellebrite/Pegasus tiles).

SELECTION, non-blocking: Q5 ("Can on-device scanning be held to one category of illegal content…") is at T2 while the Client-Side Scanning Proponent is a tier-1 above-fold camp and the EU scanning fight is the topic's why_now. Its central objection is therefore below the fold. Defensible as-is, since Q4's spread-to-authoritarians question serves the higher-prevalence Digital Rights camp, but worth a look if tiers get revisited.

Client-Side Scanning Proponent description: "It is the detection layer already running today" reads, above the fold, as if client-side scanning is deployed — while the detail records that Apple paused the rollout in 2021 and cancelled the iCloud matching component in December 2022. It is in-camp voice and the running system (server-side perceptual hashing) is a fair referent, so not blocking, but "the same detection layer moved earlier in the pipeline" would be truer to the record without weakening the steelman.

Apple/UK stat: the compact note leaves the worldwide February 2025 demand standing, while the detail records the DNI's August 2025 statement that the UK dropped it for Americans' data, the narrowed October 2025 notice, and Apple's fresh August 2026 challenge. The label is dated "UK order, 2025" so the compact line is not wrong, but a reader above the fold has a stale picture of a still-live fight.

"Years before the first backdoor mandate collapsed · US Clipper Chip": the label calls Clipper a mandate; the note more accurately calls it "the first push to mandate." Clipper was a government-pushed standard that was never legally mandated. Borderline fact territory rather than presentation, flagged for the human rather than fixed here.

why_now is a single 60-word sentence carrying four clauses (trilogue state, the voluntary-vs-mandatory split, the E2EE carve-out, the open question). Compact register asks for one idea per sentence; splitting it in two would land the same content much harder. Prose critic's territory, listed here only because it is the first thing an above-fold reader meets.

basics.stats[0].note: "counted as incidents, the drop is about 19 percent" introduces a reports-vs-incidents counting distinction that is never explained, in compact or in the detail. Not blocking (the headline 43% stands on its own), but a reader cannot tell what an "incident" is versus a report. Consider "counted as distinct incidents rather than individual reports, the drop is about 19 percent", or move the clause into the detail where the ESP breakdown already lives.

actions[0].title "EFF on encryption" is a bare acronym in a compact field. It is rescued immediately by its own description ("The Electronic Frontier Foundation's hub..."), which is why this is not blocking, but "EFF on encryption" alone would be opaque if titles ever render without descriptions.

Position descriptions sit between the two registers and carry the draft's remaining unglossed terms: "key escrow, weaker forward secrecy, or new code paths" and "Salt Typhoon" (No-Backdoor Cryptographer), "EncroChat's infrastructure" (Targeted Hacking Investigator, never identified as an encrypted phone network anywhere in the draft), "Berkman Klein's 2016 Don't Panic report" and "no single choke point" (Metadata Sufficiency Analyst). Each is partly self-glossing by the clause around it, and the details carry the real explanation, so none blocks — but EncroChat is the weakest of the four, since neither the description nor the detail says what it was.

Steelman 5, "One warrant, one endpoint, zero backdoors in everyone else's encryption": "endpoint" is mild security jargon. The parallel construction makes it read as "one device" for most readers, so it passes, but "one phone" would be free of the risk with no loss of punch.

Thinnest detail in the draft is basics.stats[6] (WhatsApp/Signal user base): its first clause re-states the note's "roughly 70 million", and its last sentence is framing rather than substance. It clears the bar on the 2020/2022 trajectory and the 220 million cumulative downloads, but it is the one detail with little headroom — a line on how monthly-active figures are counted, or on WhatsApp's 3 billion, would strengthen it.

questions[1] ('How much serious crime actually goes unsolved...'): the detail's closing sentence, "Because no public agency publishes a rigorous, audited tally of cases lost specifically to encryption versus cases solved by other means", restates the why nearly word for word. The two paragraphs above it add plenty, so this is not a restatement failure — but that closing clause is the one sentence in the field doing no new work.

basics.stats[4] (FBI/$1.3 million): the detail repeats "Comey publicly suggested the tool cost more than $1.3 million", already in the note. It earns its place on the 2017 FOIA exemption and the case timeline, so it passes; dropping the repeated attribution would make the added material land faster.

plan_positions.name: No-Backdoor Cryptographer
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: Near-unanimous in the cryptographic research literature from the 1997 key-recovery report through 2015’s Keys Under Doormats, and the operating position of every major end-to-end encrypted messaging provider, several of which have threatened market exit over it.
plan_positions.sketch: No exceptional-access design has ever survived technical scrutiny, so building one trades everyone’s security for a warrant.

plan_positions.name: Exceptional Access Mandater
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: The declared position of Five Eyes governments since their 2018 ministerial statement on access to evidence and encryption, carrying statutory footprint in the UK’s technical capability notices and Australia’s assistance and access regime, and echoed by European police leadership.
plan_positions.sketch: A judge’s order should be executable; a space no lawful warrant can reach is a product decision, not a law of nature.

plan_positions.name: Digital Rights Defender
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: Carried by UN special rapporteur submissions on privacy and expression and by the large international civil-society coalitions that mobilized against the EU scanning proposals; dominant share of the non-governmental record in the debate.
plan_positions.sketch: Whatever one democracy builds, every other government will demand, and journalists, dissidents and abuse survivors pay first.

plan_positions.name: Client-Side Scanning Proponent
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: Backed by the European Commission’s original 2022 detection-order proposal, a 2022 GCHQ and NCSC technical paper, Apple’s announced-then-withdrawn 2021 on-device design, and sustained campaigning by major child-protection organizations.
plan_positions.sketch: Check content on the device before it is sealed, and the transport encryption stays intact while abuse still gets caught.

plan_positions.name: Targeted Hacking Investigator
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: Already codified as equipment-interference and state-hacking powers in UK, German, French and Australian law, and advanced in the academic literature by senior computer scientists as the explicit alternative to systemic mandates.
plan_positions.sketch: Break into the specific suspect’s endpoint under warrant instead of weakening the cryptography protecting everyone else.

plan_positions.name: Metadata Sufficiency Analyst
plan_positions.prevalence_basis: Anchored by the 2016 Berkman Klein “Don’t Panic” report, whose signatories included former intelligence officials, and by the observation that most abuse reporting still originates on unencrypted surfaces; a persistent scholarly framing rather than a legislative bloc.
plan_positions.sketch: Investigators hold more data on more people than ever; the shortfall is resourcing and cooperation, not a missing power.
